title: Biweekly team update — November 16, 2026
jerry:
The clock frequency is now 75 MHz.

Tiling
- New registers: TILE_CFG (0x70): tile_r, tile_c, use_prev_out; CANVAS_WIDTH (0x80); TILE_ROWS / TILE_COLS (0xA0 / 0xB0).
- output_buffer is now a canvas. A matmul's WEIGHT_ROWS × INPUT_COLS result lands with its top-left corner at canvas row tile_r × TILE_ROWS, column tile_c × TILE_COLS.

Bias + GELU
- New register ACT_CFG (0x90): bias_en, gelu_en, prev_int8, out_raw.
- New bias buffer: 256 × int32, one bias per canvas row, write-only host window at 0x0800.
- New internal psum buffer: raw 32-bit sums now live here between contraction blocks. output_buffer holds only the int8 result, one byte at its canvas position, and is 64 KB (a 256×256 canvas).
- Output pipeline: sum + bias → rescale by OUTPUT_SCALE → add the previous int8 value (prev_int8) → saturate → optional GELU lookup table.
- out_raw: leaves the raw sums in the psum buffer, with no int8 written, for a later use_prev_out matmul to continue.

Smaller psum buffer
- The psum buffer went from 4096 to 1024 slots per bank and now holds a single tile, addressed relative to the tile instead of the canvas.
- Limit: a tile can hold at most 128×128 elements.

Measured throughput at 75 MHz: ECE496 Files & Data → "Matmul throughput by tile size (75 MHz)" (link below).
CPU baseline for comparison (2 threads, NEON SIMD kernel, 32×32 tiling): ECE496 Files & Data → "CPU baseline matmul throughput", with how GOP/s is calculated (2 × N³ / time).
stephanie:
TinyViT CPU–FPGA integration (Nov 17, 2026)

- MNN on the HPS CPU now runs one mixed-precision TinyViT graph and synchronously offloads 30 static-weight W8A8 matmuls: 8 QKV projections, 9 attention output projections, 9 MLP FC1 and 4 MLP FC2 operations. Dynamic QKᵀ and attention × V, softmax, normalization, residuals, convolutions and the remaining model stay on CPU.
- Four FC1→activation→FC2 pairs (stage 1 block 1; stage 2 blocks 0–2) keep hidden INT8 activations in FPGA RAM one row block at a time. A 256-entry activation LUT skips 16 intermediate CPU conversion/activation/layout operations. Fusion avoids 1.60 MB of logical hidden-tensor round trips and reduces actual host payload by about 616 KB per image; extra weight reloads account for the difference.
- The driver uses MNN’s calibrated INT8 tensors directly. FPGA matmuls complete the full INT32 reduction before per-channel fixed-point requantization. About 2.63 MB of static INT8 weights are cached in HPS DDR and tiled into FPGA RAM; the resident configuration runs 437 hardware jobs per image, without CPU/FPGA overlap.
- Mixed precision preserves sensitive operations: 7 W8A8 depthwise convolutions and 31 FP32 sensitive convolutions run on CPU. On a separate 200-image CPU holdout, mixed precision classified 148/200 correctly versus 149/200 for FP32 and 21/200 for broad quantization. This is a CPU precision-selection result, not an integrated FPGA accuracy result.

Whole-model inference (20 random RGB images, 2 CPU threads, 90 MHz FPGA, detailed profiling disabled)
- Original FP32 CPU: 1,155.982 ms mean.
- Mixed-precision CPU: 1,080.605 ms.
- Mixed precision + 30 separate FPGA operations: 1,048.245 ms.
- Mixed precision + resident FPGA pairs: 1,006.955 ms.
- Final saving: 149.027 ms (12.89%) versus FP32 CPU and 73.650 ms (6.82%) versus mixed-precision CPU. Resident fusion saves a further 41.289 ms versus separate offloads. Roughly half of the gain over FP32 comes from mixed precision and half from FPGA offload/fusion.
tiffany:
Live classification on the DE1-SoC (updated Nov 22, 2026)

The USB camera connects to the HPS USB host. Linux captures MJPEG frames through V4L2 and decodes them to RGB on the HPS. The board also preprocesses each frame and prints the predicted ImageNet class in its Linux terminal. The linked recording shows the earlier CPU-only demo that used Windows preprocessing.

Image preprocessing
- Resize the shorter side to 256 pixels using bicubic interpolation, preserving aspect ratio. Take a 224 × 224 center crop.
- Scale RGB values to [0, 1], subtract the channel means (0.485, 0.456, 0.406), and divide by the channel standard deviations (0.229, 0.224, 0.225). Supply the resulting FP32 tensor in channel-first order.

TinyViT-5M versus TinyViT-21M accuracy on HPS
- Tested both FP32 MNN models with two HPS CPU threads and zero FPGA jobs. Both received identical preprocessed tensors for 200 saved Imagenette validation images, 20 per class, and predicted across all 1,000 ImageNet classes.
- TinyViT-5M: 158/200 top-1 (79.0%) and 195/200 top-5 (97.5%).
- TinyViT-21M: 167/200 top-1 (83.5%) and 199/200 top-5 (99.5%).
- On this subset, 21M made nine more correct first-choice predictions overall, gaining 4.5 percentage points in top-1 and 2.0 points in top-5 accuracy.

The live 21M hybrid demo also ran on the board with HPS-local capture and preprocessing. Each classified frame reported 207 FPGA jobs, two offloaded linear layers and one resident MLP pair. A remaining measurement goal is to separate capture, preprocessing, transfer, inference and display time under matched conditions.
winnie:
Softmax Implementation

- Changed to signed INT8 scores/probabilities (0–127), using a 256 × 16-bit exponential LUT and 23-cycle unsigned restoring division. Supports up to 196 values per row.
- All 578 rows / 25,999 RTL outputs matched the integer reference. Standalone 90 MHz timing passed: 175 ALMs, 3 M10Ks, 0 DSPs. Ten-image relative RMSE: 6.634% for probabilities and 2.532% for P@V; long-row accuracy and probability row sums still need attention.

LayerNorm Implementation and Timing

- Built signed INT8 LayerNorm for up to 576 channels, using a 25-cycle digit-by-digit integer square root and 41-cycle restoring division. Calibrated validation relative RMSE: 3.485%.
- All 744 rows / 200,296 RTL outputs matched the integer reference. Pipeline/width optimizations preserved integer results and passed standalone 90 MHz timing: 510 ALMs, 4 M10Ks, 8 DSPs.

Next: integrate both operators with matmul and the full SoC, verify scales/data layouts and more model sites, and perform board and end-to-end testing. Neither module has been run on the board or shown full-system speedup yet.
